analysis.title: October retail sales: looking past a tepid month
key_insights: BAC card spending per HH was up 5.8% y/y in October. On a m/m SA basis it rose just 0.1%, the second consecutive month of soft sequential gains.
SA card spending declined in many retail categories in October, but a rebound in online retail (card not present, +0.7% m/m) should boost the Census retail sales figures.

The October control group seasonal factor is much less favorable than last year in the BAC card data, but the Census projected control group SF is similar to last year. BofA thinks this discrepancy raises Census October retail sales by 0.2-0.3pp relative to the signal from the BAC card data.
BofA forecasts a trend-like October retail sales report close to consensus: +0.4% m/m for both retail sales ex-autos and the control group.
Consumer fundamentals look healthy going into the holidays: strong October job growth, a low unemployment rate, gas prices that appear to have peaked, and supportive equity wealth effects.
Holiday item spending is up 7.4% relative to the same period 52 weeks ago, running well above previous years.
The share of discretionary spending in total card spending was lower in October 2026 than October 2025 across all income cohorts, which tempers BofA's optimism.
K-shaped spending has reversed. Lower-income HHs lead holiday spending growth at about 9% y/y in October, versus 6% for higher-income HHs and 4% for the top 5%.
Gen Y and Gen Z HH holiday spending is up about 10% y/y, well ahead of older households.

Transaction growth is outpacing spending growth for holiday items overall and in several categories. This could reflect a shift to online retail or consumers trading down, and BofA says it is still early and will keep watching through Nov-Dec.
Lower-income HHs have seen a disproportionate rise in non-discretionary spending (gas, groceries, utilities) since the Iran conflict started.
Total card spending was up 6.2% y/y in the week ending Oct 31 (ex-gas 5.1%). Gas spending was up 25.0% y/y, online retail 7.6% and brick-and-mortar retail 3.7%.
In the week ending Oct 31, y/y spending was negative for furniture (-4.1%) and department stores (-8.1%), and lodging was flat (0.0%). Airlines were +7.3% and general merchandise +7.2%.
Lower-income y/y clothing spending growth turned negative and higher-income lodging spending growth turned negative in the week ending Oct 31.

risk_factors: Discretionary share of spending was lower in October than last year across all income cohorts.
Transaction growth outpacing spending growth may signal consumers trading down to lower price points.
BAC card data has selection bias and excludes cash, checks and ACH payments, so it may not match Census data.
charts_described: Exhibit 1 compares BofA forecasts and Bloomberg consensus for October retail sales: headline 0.2% vs 0.1%, ex-autos 0.4% vs 0.3%, ex-autos and gas 0.4% vs 0.4%, control group 0.4% vs 0.4%.
Exhibit 2 shows BofA's retail sales ex-autos forecast correlation with Census data at 86% over the last 12 months versus 89% for consensus, and mean squared error of 0.14 versus 0.19.
Exhibit 3 shows October BAC card spending m/m SA: total 0.1%, retail ex-auto 0.0%, online retail 0.7%, furniture -2.7%, department stores -1.9%, airlines -0.8%.
Exhibit 20 shows total card spending up 6.2% y/y and ex-gas spending up 5.1% y/y in the week ending Oct 31.

tension_points.bull_case: Holiday item spending is up 7.4% from 52 weeks ago, the job market is strong, the unemployment rate is low, gas prices appear to have peaked and equity wealth effects are supportive.
tension_points.bear_case: The discretionary share of spending was lower than last year across all income cohorts, and transaction growth outpacing spending growth could mean consumers are trading down.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Continued weakness in the discretionary share and trade-down signs in the Nov-Dec data, which BofA says it will watch closely.
